ImageDescription.value:
KINGS of LYDIA. Alyattes. Circa 620/10-564/53 BC. EL Trite – Third Stater (12.5mm, 4.69 g). Sardes mint. Head of roaring lion right, “sun” on forehead; WALWET (in Lydian script) downward on right, read from outside-in; all on plain background / Two square punches.

The lion head/incuse coinage is among the earliest firmly attributed to the Lydian kingdom, and its origins date to the time of Alyattes III, who may have ruled circa 620/10-564/53 BC, according to writings by Herodotus. However, stratigraphic dating of the Artemision Hoard has shown the terminus ante quem of these coins to be closer to 630 BC. While most of the coins are anepigraphic, a small number of them bear the inscription WALWET or KUKALIM in Lydian. Hoard studies of reverse die punches have shown that these coins were not only contemprary with one another, but also with the anepigraphic issues. The linguistic study by Alexander Dale 2015 firmly concludes that the inscriptions WALWET and KUKALIM should be translated as "Alyattes" and "Male descendent of Gyges", respectively.

��All trites and hektes with the inscription WALWET or KUKALIM are struck from obverse dies that are much larger than the respective denominations require. These dies contain two opposing lion heads with the Lydian inscription between, and the coin blanks were struck off-center, in such a way that only one of the lion heads would be visible with the inscription. On the right edge of the obverse of the present coin, one may see the nose and tip of the jaw of the opposing lion head.

ObjectName.value: Panning for gold at Gold Hill, Yukon Territory, ca. 1898

Categories.value: Klondike Gold Rush|Photographs by Asahel Curtis|Images from the Museum of History and Industry|PD-old-80-expired|CC-PD-Mark|PD-old missing SDC copyright status|Gold panning in Canada|Sluice boxes

Artist.value: Asahel Curtis

ImageDescription.value:
Miners used water running through sluices to wash the gold out of the pay dirt. Larger chunks of gold and gravel settled out along the uneven bottom of the sluice boxes. The smallest pieces of gold and dirt were washed to end of the sluice box where the gold was removed by panning.

This photo, taken around 1898 by Asahel Curtis, shows a Gold Hill miner panning for gold at the end of a sluice box. Gold Hill was located near the early Klondike strike at Bonanza Creek, Yukon Territory.

9520436.title: File:Yuan dynasty banknote with its printing plate 1287.jpg

ObjectName.value: Yuan dynasty banknote with its printing plate 1287

Categories.value: Woodcuts of China|Yuan Dynasty|GFDL|Taken with Sony DSC-T10|Images with annotations|Chinese inscriptions|License migration redundant|Self-published work|13th-century woodcuts|Phagspa inscriptions|Banknotes of the Yuan dynasty|Printing plates for Chinese banknotes|Engraved woodblocks

ImageDescription.value:
Yuan dynasty banknote with its printing wood plate 1287. An upper line reads: 「至元通行寳鈔」 zhì yuán tōng háng bǎo chā (Pinyin left line: 'Phags-pa script) reads: zhì yuán bǎo chāo : to say 「至元寳鈔」. The smaller Chinese characters in the bottom half of the note say "(this note) can be circulated in various provinces without expiration dates. Counterfeiters would be put to death.
This banknote has a value of èr guàn (
貳貫
) printed on it, where 貳 is the version of the word "two" used in financial writing, and 貫 is a unit of measure called a string of cash coins. Directly under the words "貳貫" are a picture of 2 circular strings of cash coins, visually depicting the physical currency value represented by this banknote.

Credit.value: Own work, photographed at Tokyo Currency Museum
